title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project management, and the key reason being the desire for more control over their data and costs. The main difference between the two tools lies in their approach to data ownership and cost structure.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira charges a per-user fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data Ownership: Jira stores data on its servers, while Plane allows users to host their data on their own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Jira has a more complex setup process, while Plane is relatively easier to set up.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large teams and projects, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration: Jira has a built-in integration with other Atlassian tools, while Plane has an open API for custom integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Pros:
	+ Robust feature set
	+ Large user community
	+ Integrates well with other Atlassian tools
	+ Scalable
	+ Reliable customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Steep learning curve
	+ Limited customization options
	+ Data stored on Jira's servers
**Plane:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and self-hosted
	+ High degree of customization
	+ Open API for custom integrations
	+ Simple and intuitive interface
	+ Data stored on user's own servers
* Cons:
	+ Limited scalability
	+ Smaller user community
	+ Limited support resources
	+ Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance
	+ Limited built-in features compared to Jira

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams or enterprises that require a robust feature set and are willing to pay for it. It's also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the Atlassian ecosystem and want to take advantage of the integrations with other tools. On the other hand, Plane is a good choice for smaller teams or teams on a budget that want a high degree of customization and control over their data. It's also a good choice for teams that value simplicity and ease of use.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a new Plane instance on your own server.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your data from the CSV or JSON file.
4. Configure your Plane instance to match your team's workflow and needs.
5. Test your Plane instance to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's API is still in development, and some features may not be fully functional. However, for teams that value control over their data and costs, and are willing to put in the time and effort to set up and customize Plane, it may be a good choice. We recommend switching to Plane if you're a small to medium-sized team with simple project management needs and a technical team that can handle setup and maintenance.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like Gantt charts or resource allocation.
* Teams on a tight budget that can't afford Jira's per-user fees.
* Teams that value simplicity and ease of use above advanced features.
* Teams that require a high degree of customization and control over their data.
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle setup and maintenance of a self-hosted solution.

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, with no per-user fees.
### Can I migrate my data from Jira to Plane?
Yes, you can export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the import tool.
### Is Plane scalable?
No, Plane is not yet scalable to the same level as Jira, and is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
### Does Plane have built-in integrations with other tools?
No, Plane has an open API for custom integrations, but does not have built-in integrations with other tools like Jira does.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet, Plane is still in development and may not be suitable for production use by most teams.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

title: Linear vs Plane

# Linear vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Linear and Plane are both project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Linear who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of needing more control over their data or seeking a self-hosted solution. The key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and autonomy over their project management environment.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Linear offers a free plan and charges $8 per user per month for its paid plan, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data Ownership: Plane allows users to have full control over their data since it is self-hosted, whereas Linear stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain due to its self-hosted nature, whereas Linear offers a simpler, cloud-based setup.
* Scalability: Plane's scalability depends on the user's server capabilities, whereas Linear handles scalability on its end.
* Integration Difference: Plane offers more flexibility in terms of custom integrations due to its open-source nature, whereas Linear has a set of predefined integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Linear | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $8/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $400/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,600/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Linear
* Pros:
  + Easy to set up and use
  + Scalability is handled by Linear
  + Offers a free plan
  + Integrates with a variety of third-party tools
* Cons:
  + Data is stored on Linear's servers
  + Less control over custom integrations
  + Paid plan can become expensive for large teams
  + Limited flexibility in terms of customization
### Plane
* Pros:
  + Self-hosted, giving users full control over their data
  + Highly customizable and flexible
  + Free to use, with costs limited to server maintenance
  + Open-source, allowing for community-driven development
* Cons:
  + Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain
  + Scalability depends on the user's server capabilities
  + Limited support options compared to Linear
  + May require more time and resources to configure and customize

## When to Choose Each
Linear is suitable for teams of all sizes that prioritize ease of use and do not require a high level of customization or control over their data. It is ideal for teams who want a straightforward, cloud-based project management solution without the hassle of maintaining their own servers. On the other hand, Plane is designed for teams that value data sovereignty, customization, and flexibility. It is particularly suited for larger teams or organizations with the technical expertise to manage their own servers and require a high degree of control over their project management environment.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Linear in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up your Plane server and configure the necessary settings for your team.
3. Use Plane's import tool to migrate your data from the exported Linear files.
4. Customize and configure Plane to fit your team's specific needs and workflow.
5. Test the migration to ensure all data and settings are correctly transferred.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users due to its self-hosted nature and the technical expertise required for setup and maintenance. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Plane's scalability is directly tied to the capabilities of the user's server, which can become a bottleneck for large teams. For teams that value data sovereignty and have the technical resources to manage a self-hosted solution, switching to Plane can be a good choice, but for those prioritizing ease of use and simplicity, Linear might remain the better option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise seeking more control over their data
* Teams currently using Linear's free plan but needing more features and customization
* Large organizations with the resources to manage a self-hosted solution
* Teams that do not require a high level of support from the project management tool provider
* Developers or teams with experience in self-hosted solutions looking for a highly customizable project management tool

## FAQ
### Can I use Plane for free?
Yes, Plane is free to use, with costs limited to server maintenance and upkeep.
### Does Plane offer the same level of support as Linear?
No, Plane's support options are currently limited compared to Linear, which offers more comprehensive support for its users.
### Can I migrate my data from Linear to Plane?
Yes, you can export your data from Linear and import it into Plane using its import tool.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
Plane can be suitable for large teams, but its scalability depends on the user's server capabilities, which can become a limiting factor.
### Does Plane integrate with third-party tools?
Yes, Plane offers flexibility in terms of custom integrations due to its open-source nature, allowing users to develop their own integrations.

* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Google Workspace's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Google Workspace is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to self-host.

# Airtable vs NocoDB

## Overview

Flexible spreadsheet-database hybrid for organizing anything. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. NocoDB is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Airtable costs Free / $10-$20/user/month; NocoDB is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Airtable is Proprietary; NocoDB is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: NocoDB can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: NocoDB eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: NocoDB has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Airtable

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### NocoDB

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nocodb/nocodb](https://github.com/nocodb/nocodb) * ~45k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Airtable if:** Airtable is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose NocoDB if:** NocoDB is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Airtable in its standard export format, review NocoDB import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

NocoDB is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Airtable tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your NocoDB instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Airtable, switching to self-hosted NocoDB will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Airtable until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Airtable paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is NocoDB free to use?
Yes. NocoDB is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Airtable to NocoDB?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Airtable data, follow the NocoDB import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does NocoDB get regular updates?
Yes. NocoDB has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use NocoDB without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if NocoDB development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Airtable](https://airtable.com) and [NocoDB](https://nocodb.com) before making decisions.*
